title: When you miss a day
tomorrow: a Thursday sit full of strangers. why would Mai go?

lines: A MONK CRYING AT THE GATE.
cards: Mai's first two days at the program: a bus, a key card, a roommate, a studio at seven. She didn't sit once. Now it's night three, and the thought arrives: ruined already.
A monk in the old stories stood with the same thought at a gate. His name was Cula Panthaka. For months he'd tried to learn a single verse, and every new line pushed out the one before it.
His own brother, a respected monk, told him to go home. So he stood outside the monastery gate, crying. Then someone came out.

teach.h: THE BUDDHA LEADS HIM BACK IN.
teach.b: It was the Buddha. In Cula Panthaka's own verses, in the Theragatha, the Teacher touches his head, takes him by the arm, leads him back inside, and hands him a clean cloth. The commentary fills in the rest.
Sit in the sun, the Buddha says, rub this cloth, and repeat: removing dirt. As he rubs, the white cloth turns gray from his hands.
Watching it change, he understands: the mind gathers dust the same way, and it's cleaned the same way, one rub at a time. The commentary says he was awakened before the day was out.

The Dhammapada verse told with his story says it in Max Müller's words: "By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm."
An island isn't made in one day.

teach.h: AN ISLAND, MADE BY COMING BACK.
teach.b: It's made by coming back. That's the teaching under the story. Practice isn't a streak to protect.
It's a cloth you pick up again. Notice what the Buddha didn't do at the gate: no scolding, no count of the months lost.
He gave the man a next step.
Two missed days don't erase a seat, a morning or three reminders. They only mean tonight is the night for the next rub.

how: In Buddhist teaching a lapse in practice is met the way a wandering mind is met in meditation: you notice you have stopped, and you start again, without blame.

games.q: what does “when you miss a day” mean?
o: starting your practice again without blame
keeping a perfect record so no day is lost
making up missed sits with longer ones later

games.q: the story at the gate — tap the pairs.
p: led him in and gave him a cloth
white, then gray: the mind's dust

s: in Buddhism, missing days of practice cancels the progress you made
the Dhammapada's island is made by coming back, again and again.
Cula Panthaka struggled for months to learn a single verse
the commentary says each new line pushed out the one before.
the Buddha told Cula Panthaka to try harder at memorizing
he gave him a clean cloth to rub instead: a new way in, not more of the old.

games.q: a friend who keeps a daily Buddhist sit missed a week while sick. she says she'll restart on the first of the month, 'so it's clean.' what fits the story?
o: sit today, even briefly; the Buddha met failure with a next step
wait for the new month so the record looks clean
make up the missed week with extra-long sits this weekend
games.why: the Buddha didn't wait for a clean start: he handed Cula Panthaka a cloth that same day. begin again is the whole instruction.

practice: Take hold of any cloth within reach: a sleeve, a scarf, the hem of your shirt. Rub it slowly between your fingers, and with each breath, quietly begin again. When the mind wanders, that isn't failure; it's the next rub.

wordCard.voice: When you miss a day: not a broken streak, but the moment to pick up the cloth again.

carryVoice: Your line: begin again. The Buddha gave the man at the gate a cloth, not a lecture. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Dhammapada commentary on verse 25 (the story of Cula Panthaka and the cloth)

sources.q: By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.
